Selection statement: `switch (expr) { case v1: ...; break; ... default: ... }` chooses among many alternatives by the value of one expression.

The selector is an int-like (char, byte, short, int), String or enum expression. Case labels are distinct constants of that type, and default is optional. Control jumps to the matching label (or to default, or past the switch), and the case statements usually end with break. Without a break, execution falls through into the statements of the next case; default runs when no case matches.

Order: evaluate the selector once; compare it with the case constants; jump to the matching label (else default, else skip the switch). Then execute the statements from there in order, through later labels, until a break or the closing brace.
A switch statement has no value. Its result is the effect of the case(s) run: with `day = 3`, the S&W day switch prints Wed. Without breaks, day = 5 would print Fri, then Sat.
One execution evaluates the selector once (any side effect in it happens once) and runs the statements of one entry point and any cases it falls into. It changes only what those statements change.
A switch replaces an if-else chain only when every test is `expr == constant` on the same expression. Range tests such as the income-bracket chain (`income < 47450`) must stay an if-else chain.
Each case is normally ended by break, which exits the switch body. Leaving it out makes that case fall into the next. Inside a loop, that break exits the switch, not the loop.

Plan: multiway dispatch or lookup. It maps one discrete value (day number, menu choice, character) to one of several actions or results. Grouped labels (`case "apple": case "banana":`) map several values to one action.

When every case ends with break, reordering the cases does not change behaviour (labels are distinct constants). Removing one break changes behaviour for that value only. Adding a default changes only values with no matching label.

Use switch for more than two mutually exclusive alternatives decided by equality of one int, char, String or enum value. Use an if-else chain for ranges, doubles or unrelated conditions. Use an array lookup (S&W 1.4) when each case only selects a value.

items.text: The for statement is a loop that packages an initialization, a loop-continuation condition and an increment in its header around a body.

Syntax: for (<initialize>; <boolean expression>; <increment>) { <statements> }, with the three parts separated by semicolons; it is, with only a few exceptions, equivalent to <initialize>; while (<boolean expression>) { <statements> <increment>; }.
Run the initializer once; then repeatedly: test the condition (stop if false), execute the body, run the update.
A for statement has no value; the passes it makes are fixed by its header: for (int i = 1; i <= N; i++) sum += i; leaves sum = N(N+1)/2, and for (int i = 2; i <= 8; i += 2) prints 2, 4, 6, 8,.
One pass: the test reads the loop variable; the body applies its changes once; the update then changes the loop variable by its rule; the initializer changes state only once, before the first test.
The for header is exactly the three loop-control slots; the body runs after the test and before the update on each pass.
A for may be the body of another for: the inner for runs its complete set of passes for every single pass of the outer one.
for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) gives i each valid index 0..N-1 exactly once in increasing order, the standard way to process every array element.
A simulation runs a fixed number of trials with an outer for loop (for (int t = 0; t < T; t++)), each trial simulated inside the body.
In a for loop, continue skips the rest of the body and transfers control directly to the increment, then the next test; this is one of the few places where the for/while equivalence fails.
A variable declared in the for header is in scope only in the header and the body, so it cannot be used after the loop.
A fencepost loop is a for loop that handles one item (the first or last) outside the loop so that separators come out n-1 times for n items.
A flag search loop is a for loop that sets a boolean flag when some pass finds the target and leaves it set afterwards; the flag must be declared before the loop.
Plan: counted loop / counter-controlled repetition - do the body a known number of times, with the loop variable as a stepper (index, term number, trial number).

Rewriting a for as the equivalent while (init before, update at the end of the body) keeps behaviour, except that continue then skips the update and the loop variable stays in scope after the loop. Changing the bound or the step changes the pass count predictably (< to <= adds one pass).

rule broken: The three parts of a for header are separated by semicolons; commas only separate several statements inside the init or the update. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Writing for (int i = 0, i < n, i++): the compiler parses the commas as more declarators in the init and reports a syntax error.

items.text: The for statement is a loop that packages an initialization, a loop-continuation condition and an increment in its header around a body.

Syntax: for (<initialize>; <boolean expression>; <increment>) { <statements> }, with the three parts separated by semicolons; it is, with only a few exceptions, equivalent to <initialize>; while (<boolean expression>) { <statements> <increment>; }.
Run the initializer once; then repeatedly: test the condition (stop if false), execute the body, run the update.
A for statement has no value; the passes it makes are fixed by its header: for (int i = 1; i <= N; i++) sum += i; leaves sum = N(N+1)/2, and for (int i = 2; i <= 8; i += 2) prints 2, 4, 6, 8,.
One pass: the test reads the loop variable; the body applies its changes once; the update then changes the loop variable by its rule; the initializer changes state only once, before the first test.
The for header is exactly the three loop-control slots; the body runs after the test and before the update on each pass.
A for may be the body of another for: the inner for runs its complete set of passes for every single pass of the outer one.
for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) gives i each valid index 0..N-1 exactly once in increasing order, the standard way to process every array element.
A simulation runs a fixed number of trials with an outer for loop (for (int t = 0; t < T; t++)), each trial simulated inside the body.
In a for loop, continue skips the rest of the body and transfers control directly to the increment, then the next test; this is one of the few places where the for/while equivalence fails.
A variable declared in the for header is in scope only in the header and the body, so it cannot be used after the loop.
A fencepost loop is a for loop that handles one item (the first or last) outside the loop so that separators come out n-1 times for n items.
A flag search loop is a for loop that sets a boolean flag when some pass finds the target and leaves it set afterwards; the flag must be declared before the loop.
Plan: counted loop / counter-controlled repetition - do the body a known number of times, with the loop variable as a stepper (index, term number, trial number).

Rewriting a for as the equivalent while (init before, update at the end of the body) keeps behaviour, except that continue then skips the update and the loop variable stays in scope after the loop. Changing the bound or the step changes the pass count predictably (< to <= adds one pass).
